k-1.x_notes: Six problems on gridded boards at actual size, each with real mathematics at a K-1 entry point. P1 covers six shapes with blues and includes an 8-triangle trapezoid with 5 up and 3 down triangles, so it is even-area and still impossible, next to an odd-area case and tileable ones. P2: fewest greens on triangles of side 2, 3, 4 (answers 2, 3, 4). P3: find all blue coverings of a small hexagon (2) and a long hexagon (3), with spare slots. P4: fewest blocks with any pieces. The answers are 3 for the side-3 triangle (a pinwheel of three trapezoids beats the 'obvious' hexagon plus three greens), 3 for the 2x2 rhombus and 4 for the 12-triangle trapezoid. All verified. P5: a take-turns blue-block game on strips of 4, 5, 6 and 7 triangles and a hexagon (first, second, first, first, second). All correct, playable, and with a symmetry strategy to discover. P6: all 6 coverings of a 1-2-2 hexagon, drawn on half-size grids. Concise wording with block icons and one shared rule. Weaknesses: the footer has no id. P6 and the 'say why' in P1 will need adult support for kindergartners.
k-1.y_notes: Four pages of fill-the-outline puzzles at actual size with no inner grid: sailboat and cat, two fillings each of a hexagon and a 2x2 diamond, chevron-only arrow and star (both possible, checked), blue-only long hexagon, green-only side-3 triangle, then 'fill again with any pieces'. Everything is correct and the activities are concrete. However, there is no impossibility, no fewest, no find-all, so almost nothing of the outline's mathematics reaches this band. Each task is a few minutes of one-shot filling, so the group will likely run out well before 40 minutes. Picture labels (Sailboat, Cat, First filling, Another filling, Mountain) add headings. Tracing by an adult is needed to record anything.
k-1.reason: X gives K-1 genuine entry versions of both kernels plus a good game, enough for the full working time. Y is exactly the 'too dumbed down and ends too early' K-1 sheet the organizer has complained about.

grades-2-3.x_notes: A strong, well-sequenced development of kernel 1. P1 has a hexagram (tileable), an odd triangle, an even-area 7-up/5-down trapezoid (impossible) and a long hexagon. P2 adds holes: E has two up-holes and is unbalanced. F is a bowtie, balanced overall but impossible because each half is unbalanced, which shows counting is not sufficient. G is balanced and I verified it can be tiled. P3 asks for the fewest greens on triangles of side 2 to 5 at actual size, with a proof for the largest. P4 generalizes to sides 10 and 100. P5 compares chevrons in a table (they never do better; computed minima 4, 5, 4, 5). P6 asks for an invented 20-triangle connected board that needs 6 or more greens; it is solvable on the given grid with 13 up and 7 down. P7 asks for the rule for two greens on a side-2 hexagon. I checked all 144 up/down removals and every one can be tiled, so 'one up, one down' is exactly right. Statements are open and concise. Weaknesses: there is more than 40 minutes of material, an 'explain' comes with most problems, and the footer has no id.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Solid and on-kernel. P1 has four boards, but both impossible ones (A and C) are odd-area, so there is no even-area obstruction there. P2 asks for fewest-gap packings of triangles of side 2 to 5, then 'compare, what do you notice, explain why you cannot leave fewer'. P3 compares blues and chevrons on six boards with good contrasts: computed best gaps are 0/0, 0/4, 0/0, 0/2, 1/1 and 2/4. The math is correct throughout and should fill about 40 minutes. Weaknesses: many recording blanks ('Blues: __ Empty spaces: __'), board and 'Board A' labels, Problem 2 is labelled twice across pages, and fewer contrasting obstruction examples. The closing prompt 'Can you cover one purple exactly with blues?' hands over the key idea.
grades-2-3.reason: Both are correct and usable, but X's boards (even-area, holes, the bowtie) and its invention and rule-finding tasks develop the coloring argument much more fully, with open prompts. Y is thinner, more fill-in-the-blank, and gives away the chevron insight.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Ambitious and mathematically rich, with every check verified. P1 finds all 6 coverings of the 1-2-2 hexagon at actual size and explains completeness. P2 draws the flip graph and asks for the farthest pair (4). P3 builds three flip routes on an actual-size 2-2-2 hexagon from pictured coverings: I decoded them, they are valid, and the minima are 3, 4 and 8. P4 asks for a 4-flip round trip, and whether 5 or 7 work (they do not). P5 defines ribbons precisely, with L/R icons and a correct example; the definition always works. P6 proves that round trips are even and that E to F needs 8. P7 counts the 20 coverings of the 2-2-2 hexagon. P8 counts the 1-3-3 hexagon (20) by ribbons. Tasks are open, with goals not procedures. Weaknesses: far more than 40 minutes for three children. The P5 ribbon paragraph is dense. P2 makes children redraw all coverings, and P7 means drawing up to 20 tilings, which is tedious.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Correct throughout. I decoded the six cards: they are the six distinct tilings, the flip example matches cards A and B, the shortest A to F route is 4, and odd round trips are impossible. Ribbon codes and the rebuild ribbons are valid, and there is clean concrete recording with a centre-line notation. However, it never leaves the 6-tiling 1-2-2 hexagon, so flips and ribbons stay tiny and the 2-2-2 hexagon is never explored. Page 2 prints all six tilings right after Problem 1 says 'find as many as you can', which spoils the find-all task, and completeness is never asked. Ten problems break the investigation into small directed steps with Code/Card blanks. 'Write every order of two L's and two R's and match each to a card' and 'circle every neighboring RL or LR... can you make a flip there?' print the intended discoveries.
grades-4-5.reason: X carries kernel 2 through the larger hexagon to real proofs (parity, the lower bound of 8) and counting, with open tasks. Y is correct but confined to a 6-tiling board, spoils its own find-all problem, and scripts the ribbon discoveries step by step.

overall.reason: X is better in every band. Its mathematics is correct (all key answers verified), it is substantive at each level, and it is stated as open, concise tasks on actual-size boards. Y is error-free but its K-1 sheet is too thin to fill the hour and cannot be fixed in a 15-minute edit, while its 2-3 and 4-5 sheets are narrower and more scripted, with recording blanks and give-away prompts.
